subject: Climate & Environment
title: Lightning: Nature's Spark Plug
description: A micro-lesson that makes Lightning: Nature's Spark Plug usable.

hook.text: Lightning strikes Earth about 8 million times per day. Each bolt is hotter than the Sun's surface.

buildup.text: Inside a thundercloud, ice particles collide and build up static charge — positive top, negative bottom.

discovery.text: When the charge difference gets big enough, electricity arcs through the air at 300,000 km/h.

twist.text: The flash you see is actually the return stroke — electricity rushing back up from the ground.

climax.text: Lightning kills about 2,000 people per year worldwide and starts thousands of wildfires.

punchline.text: Every thunderstorm is an electric machine running on ice and gravity.

quiz.question: How many times does lightning strike Earth per day?

details.summary: Lightning occurs when charge separation within thunderstorm clouds produces an electrical potential of hundreds of millions of volts, discharging in a bolt that heats air to 30,000 degrees Celsius. It ignites wildfires, kills thousands of people, and is increasing in some regions.
details.whyItMatters: Lightning is the primary natural cause of wildfires and a significant safety hazard. Its expected increase in warmer, more convective atmospheres adds to fire and risk concerns.
takeaways: Lightning reaches roughly 30,000 degrees Celsius, five times hotter than the sun's surface
It kills roughly 2,000 people worldwide each year
Lightning-ignited wildfires are the largest and hardest to contain

faq.question: Why does lightning cause the biggest wildfires?
faq.answer: Lightning often strikes remote areas during dry thunderstorms without rain, igniting fires far from firefighting resources. These fires can burn undetected for days and in remote terrain where access is difficult, allowing them to grow very large.

faq.question: Will climate change increase lightning?
faq.answer: Research suggests a 12 percent increase in lightning frequency per degree of warming due to increased atmospheric instability and moisture. More lightning would mean more wildfire ignitions, particularly in boreal and dry western forests.
